Libyan Businesses Grapple With Nationwide Payments Outage Amid Ongoing Cyber Attack

A widespread cyber attack targeting Libya’s national payments infrastructure has disrupted economic activity across the country, with businesses, consumers and banks reporting severe transaction delays and outages since early Tuesday. As of Wednesday afternoon, the attack remains ongoing, and authorities have yet to announce when full service will be restored.

The incident, which sources say began with a coordinated assault on the Libyan Electronic Payments Network (LEPN), has left point-of-sale systems, ATMs and online banking platforms inoperative in Tripoli, Misrata, Benghazi and other major cities. The Central Bank of Libya confirmed the attack in a midday statement, urging calm and stating, “Our technical teams are working around the clock to restore services and safeguard customer funds.”

Retailers and wholesalers across the country report an abrupt halt in non-cash transactions, as many Libyans rely on cards or mobile wallets due to ongoing liquidity constraints. “We’ve had to turn away customers without cash,” said Sara El-Gadi, manager of the Tripoli-based supermarket chain Baraka Mart. “Suppliers can’t process payments, and deliveries are delayed because drivers can’t access fuel without electronic payment.”

The National Federation of Libyan Businesses estimates that over 80 percent of commercial payments have been affected, with some sectors—such as logistics, fuel distribution and telecommunications—facing acute operational challenges. “We’re seeing a domino effect,” said federation president Khaled Rahim. “Ports are unable to process invoices, truckers can’t buy fuel, and mobile airtime top-ups are disrupted.”

The Ministry of Economy has called for patience and warned against panic buying or hoarding, as supply chain interruptions began to impact availability of goods in some urban centers. Analysts at Maghreb Security Insight, a regional consultancy, describe the attack as “the most significant disruption to Libya’s digital infrastructure in recent memory,” noting that it exposes vulnerabilities amid the country’s ongoing political transition.

With many businesses resorting to manual record-keeping and cash-only sales, the National Payments Union said it is collaborating with security agencies and international partners to trace the perpetrators. Authorities have not commented publicly on the source of the attack or whether any data has been compromised.
